_provenance.why_this_source: Third-party 'good CTR' blog posts disagree wildly and cite each other. YouTube's own Help page is the only first-party statement about the actual population distribution, and it is stated as an interquartile range, which is enough to pin a full distribution.

official_quotes: Half of all channels and videos on YouTube have an impressions CTR that can range between 2% and 10%.
New videos or channels (like those less than a week old), or videos with fewer than 100 views can see an even wider range.
If a video gets a lot of impressions (such as if it appears on the Home Page), it's natural for the CTR to be lower.
It's best to compare CTRs between videos over the long-term and keep in mind how their traffic sources will affect their CTRs.

population_ctr.interpretation: 'Half of all channels and videos' between 2% and 10% == the middle 50% == the interquartile range. So p25 = 0.02 and p75 = 0.10.
population_ctr.note: mu and sigma are DERIVED from p25/p75 in model.mjs, not hardcoded here, so the derivation is auditable. mu = (ln p25 + ln p75)/2; sigma = (ln p75 - ln p25) / (2 * 0.674489). This yields a median CTR of ~4.5%.

traffic_source_ctr._source: Secondary//aggregator reporting, NOT first-party. Used only for the advisory note in the report, never in the maths.

hard_limits._note: Facts the tool must never contradict.
hard_limits.third_party_ctr_is_not_observable: YouTube exposes impressions and CTR only to a video's own owner, in YouTube Studio. There is NO public or partner API that returns CTR for someone else's video. Any tool claiming to report a competitor's real CTR is inferring or inventing it.
hard_limits.own_ctr_is_observable: The user CAN read their own true CTR in YouTube Studio (Reach tab) and feed it in via --actual-ctr to replace the modelled prior.
